stem: A non-dividend-paying stock trades at 50. A 1-year European call has a strike of 50, the continuously compounded risk-free rate is 5%, and N(d1) = 0.6368 and N(d2) = 0.5596. The BSM call price is closest to:

rationale.A: Incorrect. 3.86 forgets to discount the strike: 50 × (0.6368 − 0.5596).
rationale.B: Correct. Stock term minus the discounted, probability-weighted strike gives 5.22.
rationale.C: Incorrect. 2.31 discounts the stock term instead of the strike term.
rationale.D: Incorrect. 2.79 is the put price, K e^(−rT) N(−d2) − S0 N(−d1), not the call.

stem: A European call on a non-dividend-paying stock is worth 6.00. The stock trades at 80, the strike is 85, the option expires in 6 months and the continuously compounded risk-free rate is 3%. The value of the European put with the same strike and expiry is closest to:

rationale.A: Incorrect. 11.00 uses the undiscounted strike of 85 in put-call parity.
rationale.B: Incorrect. 2.27 reverses the signs of the stock and strike terms (c + S0 − K e^(−rT)).
rationale.C: Incorrect. Calls and puts have equal value only when the stock price equals the present value of the strike.
rationale.D: Correct. Put-call parity with the discounted strike gives 9.73.

stem: A stock trades at 40 and will pay a dividend of 0.80 in 3 months. A 6-month European call has a strike of 42. Volatility is 30% and the continuously compounded risk-free rate is 5%. Using BSM with the stock price reduced by the present value of the dividend, the call value is closest to:

rationale.A: Incorrect. 2.96 ignores the dividend and uses the full stock price of 40.
rationale.B: Incorrect. 2.65 adds the present value of the dividend to the strike rather than subtracting it from the stock price.
rationale.C: Correct. Using the dividend-adjusted stock price of 39.2099 in BSM gives 2.58.
rationale.D: Incorrect. 4.33 is the value of the corresponding put, not the call.

stem: Equity index options of the same maturity show implied volatilities of 28% for low strikes, 20% at the money and 17% for high strikes. What does this pattern most directly indicate?
options: The market assigns more probability to large price falls than the lognormal distribution in BSM implies
Low-strike options are mispriced and should be sold until implied volatilities equalize
The risk-free rate used by traders is higher for low-strike options
The BSM model is correct and realized volatility will be 28% for low strikes
explanation: If BSM held exactly, implied volatility would be flat across strikes. A downward-sloping skew means low-strike options are priced richly, consistent with a fatter left tail (crash risk) than the lognormal assumption allows.

rationale.A: Correct. The skew reflects fat left tails and crash risk that the constant-volatility lognormal model ignores.
rationale.B: Incorrect. The skew is a persistent feature of the market reflecting real tail risk, not a simple arbitrage.
rationale.C: Incorrect. All options of the same maturity use the same risk-free rate; the difference is in volatility.
rationale.D: Incorrect. A single asset cannot have different realized volatilities by strike; differing implied vols show that BSM's constant-volatility assumption fails.
